findings.reason: a node can implement exactly this miss-triggered refresh and §5's own promise ("A request is answered from the last computed result, never behind a recompute") still fails for the default-window case, so the plan needs a scheduling rule or a carry-forward of the previous interval's result.
findings.text: §5 justifies its interval with "15 minutes, which is longer than the 605.8 s the all-project computation takes, so the stored result is reused within that interval and recomputed after it", but velocity "spawns on a miss only" (line 137) and the default window's end rounds down to that same interval, so the computation is triggered by whichever request first misses — a request landing in the last ~606 s of interval N stores its result under key N after interval N+1 has begun, and the next request asks for key N+1 and misses again, so the interval exceeding the computation time does not produce the reuse the sentence claims; the binding condition is the interval exceeding the delay from the triggering request to the interval's end (or the refresh starting at the interval boundary)

findings.reason: without the completion-to-wake path named, the `fleet` event has no reachable production producer and the mechanism the done-when verifies is not the one that runs.
findings.text: the added sentence has "The refresh that stores a fleet-scoped result publishes it: it records the key's new version and wakes every open stream", but that refresh is the helper child process the section generalises from `/_checks` (`_start_check_refresh`/`_spawn_check_refresh`, reckon/serve.py:2183/2187, applied to all four routes by line 130), which cannot wake the parent process's in-process SSE streams, while line 137 gives the waking to `_FleetChangeWatch`; no path is named by which the child's store write reaches the parent's streams, and the done-when's fleet-event case stubs the computation in-process, so it passes while production emits nothing
